\subsubsection{Not Yet Verified}\label{sss:eis-open}

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{The runnable bench is not the whole channel.} Its feedback
    element is an ideal resistor set to the measured ladder value, which the
    campaign shows is worth \SI{0.019}{\percent} in the loop, and it carries no
    feedback capacitor. It is therefore faithful below the feedback pole and
    optimistic above a few kilohertz at the high-gain codes: at gain code 63 it
    reports \SI{2.73}{\percent} where the complete channel measures
    \SI{2.84}{\percent} at \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz}, and \SI{3.17}{\percent} against
    \SI{5.18}{\percent} at \SI{5}{\kilo\hertz}. It passes all \num{35} specs over
    the seven corner points, but its ideal feedback element moves
    \SI{0.01}{\percent} across them where the real ladder moves
    \SI{4.6}{\percent}, so it bounds the amplifiers and not the channel.
  \item \textbf{The code-level measurement is one frequency on one load.} The
    complete chain has been demodulated from converter codes once:
    \SI{13.587}{\kilo\hertz}, an \SI{11}{\kilo\ohm} resistive load, gain code 20
    (Section~\ref{sss:eis-accuracy}). One record costs about \num{3.5} hours of
    simulation and a decade lower in frequency costs an order of magnitude more,
    so neither the diagnostic band nor a complex load is covered at code level.
    The one complex-load record run saturated, at \SI{136}{\percent} of the
    output compliance window, and is excluded: a two-level excitation's peak
    current is set by the load's high-frequency limit \(R_u\) rather than by its
    impedance at the excitation frequency, which is what that record's gain code
    had been chosen against.
  \item \textbf{Kramers--Kronig consistency is not evidence of accuracy here.}
    The measured spectra pass at \SIrange{0.0003}{0.012}{\percent} rms, but a
    small-signal analysis of a linear network satisfies the relations by
    construction, so the test cannot fail on this data --- and on two of the
    Monte Carlo configurations the measured residual comes out \emph{below} that
    of the analytic impedance put through the identical fit, which is the direct
    demonstration that the number is the fit's floor. A spectrum carrying
    \SI{33}{\percent} of magnitude error passes, because the instrument's own
    error is itself a linear causal transfer function. The test would have power
    on a transient-derived spectrum, whose failure mode is non-stationarity;
    that is not what has been run.
  \item \textbf{The reference-modulation term is unmodelled, not absent.} The
    supply regulator whose output moved \SI{25.8}{\milli\volt} with the code word
    (Section~\ref{sss:dacr2r12-supply}) has been deleted from the channel, and
    in this deck the ladder takes its reference from an ideal
    \SI{2.5}{\volt} rail; what the excitation table measures is the ladder's own
    linearity between two codes and nothing else. On silicon the term returns in
    proportion to the impedance between the regulator and the ladder, which is a
    fifth reason the calibration impedance is not optional.
  \item \textbf{What the corner and Monte Carlo runs still do not cover.} Three
    things. The corner table is the pinned one of
    page~\pageref{p:pinned-passives}, so \(R_f\) does not
    corner and every figure taken from it is a lower bound: with the poly cornered
    too, \(R_f\) moves \(-33.4\,\%\) and \(+35.5\,\%\), the
    feedback pole at the top gain code becomes
    \SIrange{2.40}{6.61}{\kilo\hertz}, and the error above that pole moves by
    \(6\times\) --- the fresh electrode at gain code 63 and
    \SI{10}{\kilo\hertz} reads \SI{3.19}{\percent}, \SI{8.64}{\percent} and
    \SI{19.97}{\percent} at the fast, nominal and slow poly. Below the pole
    nothing moves, because a global shift in \(R_f\) moves the noise gain and
    the transimpedance together. The statistical model section likewise holds
    the feedback capacitor at typical, so no run in this section spreads the
    \SI{22}{\pico\farad}. And only the small-signal measurement was
    repeated: the delivered excitation, the demodulator and the code-level
    readout remain nominal-point results.
  \item \textbf{The electrode carries no temperature coefficient.} The cell
    model is a linear \(R \parallel C\), so the \SIrange{0}{85}{\celsius} runs
    move the amplifiers and not the interface. On silicon the charge-transfer
    resistance is strongly Arrhenius, which moves the load; since the error is a
    function of the noise gain and not of the chemistry that is a gain-ranging
    problem rather than an accuracy one --- but that is an argument here, not a
    measurement.
\end{itemize}
